title: Patterns of Deforestation and Forest Fragmentation in Ghana’s Apamprama Forest Reserve: A Remote Sensing-Based Approach
affiliations: University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR), University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR), University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR) and Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Patterns of Deforestation and Forest Fragmentation in Ghana’s Apamprama Forest Reserve: A Remote Sensing-Based Approach
detail.abstract: Forest ecosystems are vital for biodiversity, climate regulation, and community livelihoods, yet they are increasingly threatened by deforestation and fragmentation due to human activities. This study investigates spatial and temporal patterns of land use changes and forest fragmentation in the Apamprama Forest Reserve (AFR) between 1986 and 2024. The objectives of the study were to evaluate the effectiveness of machine learning in land use land cover change classification, identify spatial and temporal deforestation patterns, and assess forest fragmentation caused by illegal mining activities. Using multi-temporal Landsat imagery and Random Forest (RF) classification algorithm in Google Earth Engine (GEE), a higher accuracy was achieved throughout the study period. The study further revealed significant reductions in closed forest area cover, declining from 77% in 1986 to 39% in 2024, primarily due to illegal gold mining and land degradation. Fragmentation metrics indicated alarming trends, where forest patches increased from 2 in 1986 to 77 in 2024, while core forest areas reduced by 46%. Forest connectivity declined heavily, signaling ecosystem isolation and habitat degradation. Key drivers of these changes include illegal mining, and increased illegal logging in AFR, which has intensified the loss of critical ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration and biodiversity conservation. RF classification achieved high accuracy, demonstrating its utility for environmental monitoring. The findings highlight the need for reforestation, stricter enforcement against illegal mining, and community-inclusive conservation strategies to mitigate deforestation impacts and enhance forest resilience in Ghana. This research provides actionable insights for policymakers and practitioners addressing deforestation and forest fragmentation to preserve Ghana’s commons and natural resources.

title: Stock Price Bubbles, Inflation and Monetary Surprises
affiliations: Labcorp, Université Paris VIII Vincennes-Saint-Denis and Athens University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Stock Price Bubbles, Inflation and Monetary Surprises
detail.abstract: This paper examines how U.S. monetary policy shocks influence asset price bubbles under different inflation regimes. Using data from 1998-2023, we show that the transmission of policy is neither constant nor time-invariant. Standard local projection (LP) estimates suggest modest average effects, but including the COVID-19 period reveals that these relationships weaken. Employing time-varying local projections (TVP-LP), we document sharp shifts in transmission during the Global Financial Crisis and the pandemic, motivating a nonlinear approach. Nonlinear VAR-LP estimates uncover clear asymmetries: in high-inflation states, monetary tightening deflates bubbles by raising financing costs and constraining risk-taking; in low-inflation states, the same shocks amplify bubbles by raising expected inflation, narrowing credit spreads, and boosting equity returns. We interpret this inversion as evidence of a state-contingent speculative signaling channel, whereby tightening is perceived as a signal of stronger demand or implicit accommodation, encouraging further speculation. This mechanism highlights that safeguarding financial stability requires more than interest rate adjustments alone-it demands explicit attention to the inflationary environment and investor perceptions.

detail.title: Autocracies, Infrastructure Financing, and Credit Spreads *

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the role of autocratic restrictions on property rights in explaining debt financing of infrastructure and the associated credit spreads. We focus on two autocratic powers; the ability to restrict out-migration and the ability to expropriate output. We show how these two restrictions provide a deeper basis for the "democracy advantage," the claim that democracies obtain better financing terms than autocracies. We show theoretically and empirically that restrictions on migration enhance debt repayment, increase the degree to which infrastructure is debt financed, and reduce credit spreads while the ability to expropriate wealth has the opposite affect.

By employing a comparative analysis, it examines the approaches to sustainable development in both nations. The research objectives encompass evaluating specific environmental issues, analyzing governance frameworks, comparing sustainable development initiatives, and proposing recommendations. Through a structured exploration of water scarcity, deforestation, biodiversity loss, and air pollution, this study aims to provide insights into fostering effective environmental governance and promoting sustainability in India and Afghanistan.

Horizontal linkages among ECRs can play a role in building a reliable emotional support system. We offer four suggestions to overcome existing barriers and foster these linkages.

title: Battle of the Ages: Distributional and Aggregate Effects of Monetary Policy in a Model with Age Demographics
affiliations: London School of Economics, European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Battle of the Ages: Distributional and Aggregate Effects of Monetary Policy in a Model with Age Demographics

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We develop a model in which agents face unemployment risk, but also age and eventually retire. We study the impact of different retirement schemes on life-cycle consumption and the monetary transmission mechanism. Agents save because of a fall in income upon retirement, changes along the life-cycle wage profile, and unemployment risk. Changes in retirement policies affect the distribution of available assets (bonds) among the middle aged and the young, which in turn can have a strong impact on the ability of the young to insure themselves against unemployment risk. Interestingly, it is possible that an increase in retirement benefits leads to higher consumption levels during sustained unemployment spells even though the associated increase in taxes reduces unemployment benefits. The reason is that this policy induces the middle aged to save less which leaves more of the available asset supply to the young. A reduction in the interest rate has a bigger impact on those for whom labor market conditions improve the most and – due to a larger negative income effect – has a smaller impact on those who save more. In terms of the aggregate impact of monetary-policy shocks, our paper confirms conventional wisdom that the expansion is magnified in the presence of incomplete markets, since it is then accompanied by a fall in precautionary savings. The novel aspect of our analysis is that the extent of the incompleteness, i.e., the ability of those subject to unemployment risk to insure themselves, is endogenous. Specifically, it is reduced as the young (middle-aged) hold a larger (smaller) fraction of the available asset supply and this distribution is not only affected by retirement policies, but also by government bond supply and the life-cycle wage profile. Thus, understanding the distribution of assets across different age cohorts is not only important for understanding life-cycle consumption patterns, but also business cycles.

title: Estimating Time Discount Rates for Covid-like Diseases Vaccination: from a Discrete Choice Experiment in Wuhan
affiliations: and University of Texas at Dallas

detail.title: Estimating Time Discount Rates for Covid-like Diseases Vaccination: from a Discrete Choice Experiment in Wuhan

detail.abstract: This study explores the temporal preferences for the vaccination of COVID-like diseases (CLD) in Wuhan, China, through a discrete choice experiment (DCE). Unlike previous literature, which relied on stated preference method with limited real-world applicability, this research uses the DCE method to simulate realistic decision making. The study uniquely uses the DCE approach to estimate and compare hyperbolic and exponential discount rates for CLD vaccination, which fills critical gaps in the use of DCE to calculate temporal discount rates for vaccination. Our results show a steep discount rate in the vaccination of CLD for hyperbolic (0.225) and exponential (0.16) compared to previous research. The discount rate for CLD vaccination shows heterogeneity in demographics, health behaviors, health conditions, and levels of government trust. We do not find significant differences in gender, medical resources, and previous vaccine reaction. Some customized policy insights aimed at building immediate herd immunity for future outbreaks are informed by the findings of this study.

title: How is Subjective Financial (in)Security Related to Household Stress Prevalence and Intensity?
affiliations: TIAA Institute

detail.title: How is Subjective Financial (in)Security Related to Household Stress Prevalence and Intensity?

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Stress has a significant impact on health outcomes. And while the connection between health and wealth is well studied, the connection between financial security and stress is less studied. We examine how self-reported financial security is related to reported stress across 11 household areas with survey evidence. We find subjective financial security is highly correlated to self-reported stress. Individuals reporting relatively lower financial security are significantly more likely to report stress and do so across more areas and with greater intensity. When controlling for financial security, there are limited stress differences between males and females on the extensive margin, with some differences in intensity. There are no significant financial security differences by age, but younger individuals are more likely to report stress with greater intensity. Differences across age groups may be explained by younger workers having greater lifecycle uncertainty compared to older workers. Household income has little explanatory power once controlling for financial security. Our results highlight the importance of subjective measures, and how subjective financial measures impact life in other domains, and the importance of benefit programs that promote financial security and stress management.

title: Do Misperceptions About Medicare Coverage Explain Low Demand for Long-Term Care Insurance?
affiliations: Department of Economics, University of South Florida, Swarthmore College, Swarthmore College, University of South Florida and Independent

detail.title: Do Misperceptions About Medicare Coverage Explain Low Demand for Long-Term Care Insurance?

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Long-term care represents a significant financial risk for elderly individuals. Despite this risk, only 14% of those age 60 and over have private long-term care insurance (LTCI), and about one-third of all longterm care expenses in the United Staes are paid for out of pocket. In this study, we examine whether misperceptions about Medicare coverage explain the low demand for LTCI. Surveys of older Americans find that about 40% of individuals believe that Medicare will pay for long-term care. However, Medicare only provides limited coverage of short-term stays in skilled nursing facilities following a qualifying hospital stay. Using a regression discontinuity design (RDD) based on eligibility for Medicare at age 65, we document a statistically significant increase in private LTCI coverage rates at the time of enrollment in Medicare. A potential explanation for this increase is that, during the process of enrolling in Medicare, individuals learn that Medicare doesn't cover long-term care services and consequently purchase private LTCI. Using data from two unique surveys on planning for long-term care, we also find that knowledge of Medicare coverage of long-term care services improves at age 65, providing support for the misperception hypothesis.

title: Q-Learning–Driven Adaptive Rewiring for Cooperative Control in Heterogeneous Networks
affiliations: National Taiwan University and Lehigh University

detail.title: Q-Learning–Driven Adaptive Rewiring for Cooperative Control in Heterogeneous Networks
detail.abstract: Cooperation emergence in multi-agent systems represents a fundamental statistical physics problem where microscopic learning rules drive macroscopic collective behavior transitions. We propose a Q-learning-based variant of adaptive rewiring that builds on mechanisms studied in the literature. This method combines temporal difference learning with network restructuring so that agents can optimize strategies and social connections based on interaction histories. Through neighbor-specific Q-learning, agents develop sophisticated partnership management strategies that enable cooperator cluster formation, creating spatial separation between cooperative and defective regions. Using power-law networks that reflect real-world heterogeneous connectivity patterns, we evaluate emergent behaviors under varying rewiring constraint levels, revealing distinct cooperation patterns across parameter space rather than sharp thermodynamic transitions. Our systematic analysis identifies three behavioral regimes: a permissive regime (low constraints) enabling rapid cooperative cluster formation, an intermediate regime with sensitive dependence on dilemma strength, and a patient regime (high constraints) where strategic accumulation gradually optimizes network structure. Comparative analysis against Bush-Mosteller stimulusresponse learning demonstrates that Q-learning’s temporal credit assignment capabilities produce superior cooperation outcomes, particularly under intermediate rewiring constraints where long-term relationship assessment becomes crucial. Simulation results show that while moderate constraints create transition-like zones that suppress cooperation, fully adaptive rewiring enhances cooperation levels through systematic exploration of favorable network configurations. Quantitative analysis reveals that increased rewiring frequency drives large-scale cluster formation with power-law size distributions. Our results establish a new paradigm for understanding intelligencedriven cooperation pattern formation in complex adaptive systems, revealing how machine learning serves as an alternative driving force for spontaneous organization in multi-agent networks.

title: Is Baldness Inequality an Analogy for Income Inequality in General Equilibrium?

detail.title: Is Baldness Inequality an Analogy for Income Inequality in General Equilibrium?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or animals, and therefore ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: We develop an analytic analogy between "baldness inequality" and income inequality to isolate three portable mechanisms: inherited asymmetries with cumulative dynamics, unequal access to mitigation, and aggregate feedback. A basic dynamic law S t+1 = α(1θm)S t + ε t nests heterogeneity, budget constraints, intergenerational learning, and generalequilibrium externalities. Synthetic illustrations show how the composite parameter φ = α(1-θm) governs trajectories and how regressive externalities raise α t , slowing convergence. Policy implications follow directly: early interventions that raise θm at the bottom and reduce regressive externalities are jointly necessary for sustained reductions in S t. A light empirical anchoring (Appendix B) calibrates plausible values and demonstrates robustness to ±10% variation. The framework is parsimonious yet extensible, yielding falsifiable comparative statics and an operational targeting rule. Limits of the analogy are explicit: domains are not ontologically equivalent, and welfare ramifications of income extend beyond the psychosocial effects of baldness.

detail.title: Visibly Fair Mechanisms

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW - Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 25-048

detail.abstract: Priority-based allocation often requires eliminating justified envy, making serial dictatorship (SD) the only non-wasteful direct mechanism with that property. However, SD's outcomes can conflict with the policymaker's objectives. We introduce visible fairness, a framework where fairness is evaluated using coarser information. This is achieved by designing message spaces that strategically conceal information that could render desired allocations unfair. We characterize these mechanisms as generalizations of SD, establish conditions for strategy-proofness, and show how to implement distributional constraints. This creates a new trade-off: achieving distributional goals may require limiting preference elicitation, forgoing efficiency gains even when compatible with the constraints.

title: Beyond the Deal: Towards Equity in Music

detail.abstract: Artists and record labels are the key players in the music industry. While artists' creativity drives the industry, investments by record labels fuel and control it. As a result of this pivotal relationship, the industry is private in nature, as the relationship between the parties is largely regulated by their contract. In recent years, issues of fair deals, ambiguous clauses, perpetual assignment of copyrights, artist images, stage names, etc., as well as restrictive music contracts, have always been in the news. These issues threaten the industry, increase the risk for potential investors, and complicate the relationship between artists and labels. Hence, the need to address these issues is paramount for the good of the industry.

title: The Youth Inflation Index: An Empirical Study of Financial Behaviour and Attitudes in Indian Youth
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Youth Inflation Index: An Empirical Study of Financial Behaviour and Attitudes in Indian Youth
detail.abstract:
Indian inflation has reshaped young adults' financial behaviour, yet very few have examined their distinct responses to higher prices. This work introduces the Youth Inflation Index (YII), a composite indicator designed to capture how young Indians aged 12–22 balance saving, expenditure, and awareness of inflation. With survey data from 59 respondents from urban India, YII integrates behavioural and economic dimensions, including the status of pocket money where savings are stored, level of financial confidence, and awareness of inflationary pressures.

The findings indicate that a substantial proportion of young adults are in the "moderate resilience" range, evidencing substantial variations by age, saving behaviour, and availability of formal instruments. Older adolescents and users of banking programs or products have higher resilience, while younger adolescents and savings-in-cash groups are found to have higher risk levels. Qualitative responses in particular emphasised peer influences, electronic pay-in mechanisms, and limited financial literacy.

The research highlights the value of targeted financial literacy, regular allowances, and structural availability of banking and investment instruments. By proposing the YII, this work offers a usable model for youth financial resilience in inflationary environments and opens pathways for policy and teaching interventions.

title: A Financial Analysis and Valuation of DIAGEO PLC

detail.title: A Financial Analysis and Valuation of DIAGEO PLC

keywords: Free Cash Flow to the Firm Model

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive financial analysis and valuation of Diageo plc, a leading global player in the Total Beverage Alcohol (TBA) sector. The primary objective is to assess the intrinsic value of Diageo's equity and provide strategic insights for potential and existing investors. Employing a multi-method valuation framework-including the Dividend Discount Model (DDM), Earnings and Investment Model (EIM), Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) model, and Price-to-Earnings (P/E) multiples approach-the study triangulates Diageo's fair market value as of 30 June 2024. The results suggest a convergence of intrinsic values around the market price of £24.08, indicating fair pricing. To enrich this valuation, the study incorporates a detailed ratio-based financial health assessment. Eight key financial ratios spanning profitability, liquidity, efficiency, and solvency dimensions are analysed using longitudinal and peer benchmarking against four comparable firms: Pernod Ricard, Brown-Forman, Constellation Brands, and Campari. Data is sourced from Capital IQ and verified using author-calculated figures, ensuring methodological rigour. Despite the observed fair pricing, the study identifies several underlying investor concerns, including Diageo's modest net income CAGR (1.38%) and a negative abnormal buy-and-hold return (-34.67%) over the 2021-2024 period. These findings indicate potential macroeconomic or sector-specific headwinds. Nevertheless, the analysis suggests that current investors may benefit from a stabilised entry point, while future valuation upside depends on operational efficiency and margin expansion. The study concludes that Diageo remains a credible long-term investment for incomeseeking investors, supported by its defensive sectoral positioning and stable dividend record. At the same time, value and growth-focused investors may require stronger catalysts before engaging. Overall, this paper contributes a multidimensional evaluation of Diageo's financial positioning and market prospects, with actionable implications for diverse investor profiles.

title: Performance of Energy ETFs and Climate Risks
affiliations: , Deakin University and University of Hull

detail.title: Performance of Energy ETFs and Climate Risks
detail.abstract: We investigate whether green (brown) portfolios constructed from clean energy ETFs (fossil fuel ETFs) yield positive (negative) returns conditional on climate-related risks. While the green portfolios do not unconditionally outperform the brown ones, the outperformance of green portfolios is statistically significant under the conditional setting using non-parametric estimates with imposing inequality restrictions. Our conditional studies also show that brown portfolios are riskier than green ones with various measurements. We present the heterogeneity in the effect of climate information on the return and risk of green and brown portfolios. Furthermore, we document that fund flows for green assets are higher than those for brown ones during periods of high climate risks. Our findings are robust to alternative specifications.

title: Weekend Information Gaps and Systemic Risk Transmission to Oil Markets: A COVOL-Based Analysis
affiliations: University College Dublin, Dublin City University , Institute for Policy Research (IPR), University of Bath and

detail.title: Weekend Information Gaps and Systemic Risk Transmission to Oil Markets: A COVOL-Based Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the transmission of systemic risk to international oil markets by analysing the dynamic connectedness between three distinct Common Volatility (COVOL) measures — Energy, Asset, and Country — and five major oil benchmarks. Utilising a framework using Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregression (TVP-VAR), EGARCH, and wavelet coherence analyses, we investigate the presence and characteristics of day-of-the-week effects in these risk relationships. Our findings consistently identify a significant Monday effect, characterised by a pronounced reduction in the dynamic connectedness between the COVOL measures and the analysed oil markets. This weekend-generated discontinuity in information flow is highly state-dependent. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the effect dissipated for Energy and Asset COVOL but intensified for Country COVOL. In contrast, during periods of geopolitical conflict, the negative signal disconnect for Asset and Country COVOL extended into Tuesday, while the effect for Energy COVOL vanished entirely as energy news became part of a continuous, high-alert information stream. Wavelet co- herence analyses corroborate these findings, revealing distinct and evolving lead-lag dynamics and demonstrating significant heterogeneity across the individual oil benchmarks, reflecting their unique sensitivities to regional, consumer, and macroeconomic shocks. The results indicate a hierarchy of influence, where country-level systemic risks exert the strongest effect on oil markets, followed by energy- and asset-level risks.

title: Artificial Identity: How Instructor Race and Gender Influence Student Behavior and Performance in AI-Mediated Learning
affiliations: Yale University - Law School and Yale University - Law School

detail.title: Artificial Identity: How Instructor Race and Gender Influence Student Behavior and Performance in AI-Mediated Learning
detail.abstract:
As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms education, AI-generated instructors offer unprecedented opportunities to scale and personalize learning. Yet, the influence of instructor identity—especially race and gender—remains underexplored in AI-driven contexts. This study provides one of the first randomized controlled experiments examining how instructor identity shapes student engagement, academic performance, and willingness to pay when instructional content is held constant. Leveraging a large-scale field experiment involving over 2,500 students enrolled in an online Coursera course, we randomly assigned students to video instruction with identical content delivered by either a human professor or one of four AI avatars whose appearance varied by race (Black or White) and gender (male or female). 

The main findings are: First, the avatars were rated similarly to the human professor in teaching effectiveness, and many avatar-instructed students reported that their instructors were likely to be human. There were no significant “man vs. machine” differences in student attrition or grades between the White-male human instructor and the White male avatar. Second, the Black male avatar outperformed the White male avatar with regard to overall course grade (p. = .047), average quiz grade (p. = .099), and number of course items completed (p. = .099). Third, female students that were assigned to female avatars received significantly higher average quiz grades (p. = .042) than those assigned to male avatars. Hispanic students who were assigned to Black avatars were significantly less likely to complete the course (p. = 041) but more likely to have a higher course grade (p. = .043) than Hispanic students assigned to White avatars.

title: Reading the Panic: How Investors Perceived Bank Risk During the 2023 Bank Run
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York,  and Federal Reserve Bank New York

detail.title: Reading the Panic: How Investors Perceived Bank Risk During the 2023 Bank Run

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The bank run that started in March 2023 in the U.S. occurred at an unusually rapid pace, suggesting that depositors were surprised by these events. Given that public data revealed bank vulnerabilities as early as 2022:Q1, were other market participants also surprised? In this post, based on a recent paper, we develop a new, high-frequency measure of bank balance sheet risk to examine how stock market investors’ risk sensitivity evolved around the run. We find that stock market investors only became attentive to bank risk after the run and only to the risk of a limited number (less than one-third) of publicly traded banks. Surprisingly, investors seem to have mostly focused on media exposure and not fundamentals when evaluating bank risk. In a companion post, we examine how the Federal Reserve’s liquidity support affected investor risk perceptions.

title: Expanding Black Reparations with Human and Social Capital Investments
affiliations: Marquette University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Expanding Black Reparations with Human and Social Capital Investments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Disadvantaged social groups in the US suffered disproportionately in the covid pandemic and Great Recession, worsening high levels of inequality associated with their post-1980 declining intergenerational income mobility. For black Americans this reflects the long history of racial discrimination beginning with slavery. Reparations paid to descendants of enslaved individuals to eliminate the black-white wealth gap is a step toward addressing this history. A further needed step is to build predominantly black communities human and social capital through public investments in community health care centers (CHCs) and historically black colleges and universities (HBCUs). There is considerable evidence that investments in early childhood education positively affect later school performance, income and earnings, higher education, crime, and other well-being outcomes. CHCs and HBCUs promote early childhood education. This paper argues compensation is due to both individuals and their communities, and reparations payments should be accompanied by public investments in those communities.

title: Good to (not) know: A Positive Impact of Non-Financial Uncertainty
affiliations: Université du Havre, Paris Nanterre University and Centre d’Economie de l’Université Paris Nord (CEPN) – UMR 7234 CNRS-Université Sorbonne, Paris 13.

detail.title: Good to (not) know: A Positive Impact of Non-Financial Uncertainty
detail.abstract: We investigate conditions under which uncertainty may have a positive effect on the economy. Contrary to what the few papers that find a positive effect, we conjecture that uncertainty may be positive not only when it is about industrial prospects but more generally when it is non-financial. To argue this, we propose a theoretical intuitive demonstration that may explain why uncertainty may be positive building on recent works on behavioral new Keynesian models: Uncertainty increases agents’ myopia and more myopia helps escape Ricardian equivalence hence implying a more positive impact of a stimulus. Then, the impact of uncertainty shocks according to their nature is studied applying local projection methods in a nonlinear framework. Uncertainty may be non-financial or financial in different regimes of general uncertainty: high, moderate and low. We get a positive and significant effect of the non-financial uncertainty shocks when the general level of uncertainty is high or moderate.

detail.abstract: This appendix explains the foundations of the Third Generation in International Relations (IR3). It shows how international relations moved step by step: from IR1 (sovereignty and institutions) to IR2 (globalization), then IR2⁺ (populist disruption), and finally to IR3 (algorithmic diplomacy). The main idea is simple: earlier generations changed the appearance of diplomacy but not its core. Institutions, globalization, and social media made diplomacy look modern, but wars, inequality, and political bias continued. This is why peace processes often failed. IR3 is different. It places algorithms, digital tools, and symbolic codes at the heart of diplomacy. The goal is not just faster communication, but real reform of the rules of global governance. By combining technology with diplomacy, IR3 offers a new way to deal with today’s challenges—such as cyber conflicts, media influence, and the loss of trust in international institutions. This appendix provides the key terms and ideas needed to follow future studies on IR3. It is both a guide to past failures and a roadmap for building a stronger and fairer system of international relations in the digital age.

detail.title: Closing Early Math Gaps by Parental Education with Technology at Home

detail.abstract: Early math skills predict later achievement, and caregiver engagement is central to early skill development. We conducted a six-month experiment (About TIME) with 459 Chicago families of preschoolers (ages 3-5) spanning the socioeconomic spectrum. Families were randomized into: a control group that received a coloring book unrelated to math, a treatment group that received a digital tablet with math apps, and a treatment group that received analog math learning materials. On average, neither type of math material significantly increased children's math skills. Pre-registered heterogeneity analyses by parental education, household income, and baseline skills show that children of non-BA parents assigned to the math app group gained 0.17 SD (about five national percentile points), while their BA-parent counterparts showed no gains, closing roughly one-third of the initial education-based skill gap. We found no significant effects in the income-based or baseline-skill subgroups. Benchmarking to our prior MPACT study (Mayer et al., 2023), we restrict About TIME to children from publicly subsidized preschools (MPACT's recruitment source) and detect a math app effect of 0.16 SD, closely matching MPACT's math app effect of 0.20 SD. These findings demonstrate a robust, replicable benefit of providing math apps to disadvantaged families of preschoolers and suggest that at-home technology may help reduce early math skill gaps.

title: Governing Schools in Times of Pandemic: A Set-Theoretical Analysis of the Role of Policy Capacities in School Closure
affiliations: Leiden University, University of Bath and IESEG School of Management

detail.title: Governing Schools in Times of Pandemic: A Set-Theoretical Analysis of the Role of Policy Capacities in School Closure
detail.abstract: Policy capacity plays a pivotal role in shaping the extent of global governmental responses to the COVID‐19 pandemic. While scholars have primarily examined this phenomenon through individual case studies, focusing on demographic variables that influence governments' COVID‐19 responses, little understanding exists regarding how existing policy capacities (systemic, organizational, and individual) have either constrained or empowered governments to navigate the pandemic diversely. To address this gap, our study focuses on the worldwide patterns of school closures and re‐openings during COVID‐19. Utilizing configurational analysis on data from 110 countries, we reveal that factors such as less professional organizational capacities, flawed individual leadership capacities, and contextual factors such as heightened political polarization serve as quasi‐sufficient conditions for longer school closures, while their significant presence leads to extended periods of schools remaining open. The research is supported by detailed case studies of the US, Colombia, Israel, and South Korea, elucidating diverse policy trajectories and combinations influencing prolonged closures or swift re‐openings.

title: When ESG Hurts: Environmental Policy and ESG Retreat in China’s Institutional Investors
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) and Chongqing Technology and Business University

detail.title: When ESG Hurts: Environmental Policy and ESG Retreat in China’s Institutional Investors
detail.abstract: We empirically examine how institutional investors react to adjustments in environmental policies in China. We observe a seemingly counterintuitive phenomenon: when environmental policies intensify, rather than tilting further toward high ESG-rated stocks, institutional investors retreat from such positions. This behavior stems from the fact that, under stringent environmental policies, maintaining a high level of ESG investing leads to financial losses and fund outflows, especially in the short term, which impair fund managers’ compensation and raise career concerns. Further, within the context of environmental policy adjustments, our heterogeneity analysis tries to disentangle the true motivations behind institutional investors’ ESG adoptions. We demonstrate that both pro-social preferences and financial incentives play pivotal roles, and that fund managers do not tolerate unlimited financial losses when ESG investing underperform. Our findings reveal the economic impact of environmental policies on institutional investors and shed light on the contentious and complex nature of the ESG concepts.

title: A Historical Perspective on Stablecoins

detail.abstract: Digital currencies have grown rapidly in recent years. In July 2025, Congress passed the “Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act” (GENIUS) Act, establishing the first comprehensive federal framework governing the issuance of stablecoins. In this post, we place stablecoins in a historical perspective by comparing them to national bank notes, a form of privately issued money that circulated in the United States from 1863 through 1935.

detail.abstract: Based on a microsimulation model developed at the Banco de España, this article quantifies the possible revenue impact of certain hypothetical changes in the configuration of inheritance and gift tax (IGT) in Spain. Takeaways • In 2023 IGT revenue amounted to 0.23% of GDP in Spain, slightly above the European Union (EU) average of 0.15%. • However, IGT revenue varies considerably across the Spanish regions, as the regional governments have the power to modify the tax parameters. • Using a microsimulation model, we estimate that, if all the regional governments were to set IGT at the levels envisaged in the State benchmark legislation, the revenue raised could increase by 0.5 percentage points (pp) of GDP to 0.7%. • This is assuming that the tax changes would not lead to substantial changes in economic agents' behaviour.

title: ESG Performance and Firm Risk: The Case of the U.S. Oil and Gas Industry
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Washington State University and Brooklyn College, The City University of New York

detail.title: ESG Performance and Firm Risk: The Case of the U.S. Oil and Gas Industry
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between ESG performance and firm risk in the U.S. oil and gas industry, a sector characterized by high volatility, regulatory exposure, and environmental scrutiny. Using panel data from 2010 to 2022, we analyze how overall ESG ratings and their environmental, social, and governance components relate to total, systematic, and idiosyncratic risk, as well as one-year buy-and-hold stock returns. We find robust evidence that stronger ESG performance - particularly governance - is associated with lower firm risk across multiple dimensions. However, ESG scores do not predict higher short-term returns, and in the case of governance, are linked to modestly lower one-year abnormal returns. These findings highlight ESG’s primary role as a mechanism for risk mitigation rather than as a source of immediate shareholder gains. The study contributes to the literature by offering the first comprehensive evidence on ESG’s risk implications in U.S. oil and gas, providing practical insights for investors, managers, and policymakers.

title: Political Power and Collectivism: The Persistent Impact of Exposure to Historical Centralized Political Regimes
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC), Independent Researcher and

detail.title: Political Power and Collectivism: The Persistent Impact of Exposure to Historical Centralized Political Regimes

keywords: Centralized Chinese Dynasties JEL Classification: P48

detail.abstract: Understanding the determinants of collectivism is essential, as it shapes economic behavior, institutional development, and social interactions. This paper identifies a novel determinant of collectivism: exposure to centralized political power. The identification compares individuals from the same birth cohort within a province, exploiting variation in county distances to historical Chinese national capitals, instrumented by proximity to the initial territorial centroids of ten centralized dynasties. Using data from the 2005 China census, we find that individuals residing in counties closer to historical capitals of centralized regimes exhibit stronger collectivist orientation than cohort peers in more distant counties within the same province. The finding is robust to alternative measures of collectivism and exposure to centralized regimes, more conservative inference approaches, and the inclusion of additional covariates. We also find that the effect varies across regions and between the periods before and after the PRC's establishment in 1949, but not by gender.

title: Macroeconomic Fundamentals and Household Stock Market Investment Decisions: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, International University of Japan and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Macroeconomic Fundamentals and Household Stock Market Investment Decisions: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: We apply machine learning techniques to assess how macroeconomic fundamentals influence U.S. households’ investment decisions for both market entry (extensive margin) and equity share (intensive margin). Using SCF data from 1992–2022, SHAP analysis shows that middle-aged, moderately risk-averse, and highly educated households place considerable weight on macroeconomic factors. In particular, among the top 50 percent of the wealth distribution, these factors are the primary drivers of market entry. We further estimate implied marginal effects, confirming that micro-level variables align with existing empirical findings while also uncovering nonlinear patterns that conventional empirical models typically overlook.

title: Whispers in the Wind: The Erosion of Transparency in Government Warnings
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, Duke University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Whispers in the Wind: The Erosion of Transparency in Government Warnings
detail.abstract: We examine how a government agency should design dynamic warning policies to guide public responses to an impending disaster. The government receives a sequence of advance signals with increasing accuracy leading up to the potential disaster, and decides what information to provide to the public. The public subsequently chooses whether to take preemptive action or delay the action. Methodology/Results: We model the setting as a two-period Bayesian persuasion game and solve the government's information design problem by tracking the public's expected utility-to-go. We find that when the government prioritizes the economic costs of taking action, alert strategies will become less or increasingly transparent over time, depending on whether the early signal is informative for the government. In contrast, when the government's and the public's incentives are well aligned, the government always discloses information with increasing transparency. Managerial implications: Our analysis rationalizes many anecdotal incidents across various settings and offers theoretical guidance for governments to issue public warnings against potential disasters.

title: Choice elasticity and local information: Evidence from patient mobility for hip replacement surgeries
affiliations: Vienna University of Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Choice elasticity and local information: Evidence from patient mobility for hip replacement surgeries
detail.abstract: Introducing competition into public healthcare systems by allowing free provider choice is a common policy measure intended to increase treatment quality. Its effectiveness, however, depends on how patients process and act upon quality signals and travel for care. Even where official quality indicators exist, they are often not easily accessible or interpretable to patients, especially the rural elderly, who may instead rely on local information channels and behavioural heuristics. We investigate how provider choice for elective hip replacement surgery in Italy is shaped by both official and informal quality signals. Exploiting a dataset of all elderly Italian patients undergoing elective hip replacement surgery between 2010 and 2015, we estimate a patient-level random utility choice model. On average, patients select hospitals with lower overall in-hospital mortality, indicating responsiveness to global quality. At the same time, we document strong neighbourhood volume effects: patients are more likely to choose hospitals where other residents from their municipality were treated, independent of quality. Finally, among rural patients who travel more than two hours for surgery—a group facing higher search costs and more deliberate decision-making—we find evidence of neighbourhood quality effects, as they are less likely to select hospitals where neighbours previously experienced adverse outcomes. These findings highlight that patient choice is shaped not only by formal indicators of quality, but also by social interaction, GP mediation, and behavioural heuristics - factors that shape regional disparities in access and outcomes.

title: Assessing the Short- and Long-Term Impacts of Market-Based Carbon Policies on Carbon Emissions: A Cross-Country Panel Data Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, National Defense University and Baskent University

detail.title: Assessing the Short- and Long-Term Impacts of Market-Based Carbon Policies on Carbon Emissions: A Cross-Country Panel Data Analysis
detail.abstract: Market-based carbon pricing systems, which integrate environmental responsibility with economic incentives, have emerged as innovative financial mechanisms in the fight against climate change. The main objective of this study is to analyze the effectiveness of market-based carbon pricing mechanisms — specifically carbon taxes and Emissions Trading Systems (ETS) — in reducing carbon emissions in both the short and long term. Using data from 31 countries between 2000 and 2023, the analysis incorporates explanatory variables into a panel ARDL model to estimate the separate and joint effects of carbon tax and ETS policies. The findings reveal that carbon taxes are more effective than ETS in reducing emissions in the long run, while the combination of both instruments yields a synergistic effect in countries that implement them concurrently. However, both policies appear to cause temporary increases in emissions in the short run, which are associated with time lags, structural adjustment costs, and behavioral responses. The effectiveness of carbon pricing becomes statistically significant particularly after the second lag period. Furthermore, causality tests indicate a dynamic and bidirectional relationship between carbon policies and emissions. Overall, the study highlights that market-based carbon policies are effective long-term tools for reducing emissions, and the limited effectiveness of ETS compared to the combined use of both instruments offers valuable insights for policymakers.

title: The Dual Burden of Energy Poverty and Climate Exposure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Dual Burden of Energy Poverty and Climate Exposure
detail.abstract: Households in the United States face compounded risks when high energy burdens intersect with heightened exposure to climate extremes. This study introduces a methodological framework to identify and analyze these dual-vulnerability households systematically. Using the 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey (RECS) linked with high-resolution NASA Daymet climate data, I spatially match households to localized measures of extreme climates like heatwaves and cold spells. Geospatial hotspot analysis reveals regions where economic and climatic risks converge, while Local Linear Forest models are employed to identify the primary drivers of household energy expenditures. The results show that climate-related variables, such as extreme temperature events and degree days, together with housing characteristics, have a stronger influence on energy costs than income. Policy simulations of interventions, including appliance upgrades, weatherization, smart home technologies, and financial assistance programs, demonstrate heterogeneous effects across household types, with technology-based strategies delivering the largest reductions in energy expenditures. These findings highlight the importance of regionally tailored, climate-responsive policies that integrate technical upgrades with socioeconomic support to enhance resilience among households at the intersection of energy poverty and climate risk.

title: Danone's Dismissal of its CEO: Risk-Return Trade-off or Risk-Return Sustainability Tripod? The Inclusion of Sustainability in the Financial Equation
affiliations: ESCP Business School

detail.title: Danone's Dismissal of its CEO: Risk-Return Trade-off or Risk-Return Sustainability Tripod? The Inclusion of Sustainability in the Financial Equation

publicationDetails.journalName: ESCP Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In March 2021, the CEO of Danone, well known for his commitment to sustainability, was dismissed due to poor financial performances. Drawing on this apparent opposition between financial and non-financial indicators, we introduce a risk-return-sustainability tripod to analyse this decision from the shareholders' point of view. We show that even for a "responsible" shareholder, financial indicators still matter, and that an equilibrium is required between the three parameters of the tripod. By applying this tripod to two different sectors, we show that various shareholder segments can co-exist in a company's capital.

title: SENDAS: Scalable ENrichment for mobility DAta Sets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: SENDAS: Scalable ENrichment for mobility DAta Sets
detail.abstract: Recent technological advancement and popularization have grown the availability of mobility data, collected from different sources. Extracting knowledge from such large amounts of data is an active research and industrial issue, with a diverse range of applications. However, existing tools currently lack scalability. Moreover, some important features are not available in such tools. To cover this gap, we introduce SENDAS – Scalable ENrichment for mobility DAta Sets – a new framework enabling parallel and distributed execution for mobility analysis techniques. We present definitions extending and improving the efficiency of state-of-the-art methods to extract stay points, areas of interest, semantic motifs, origin-destination flows, among other metrics. The performance results reveal that it was possible to speed up the processing time up to 8.6 times when compared to existing solutions in large-scale datasets. In addition, we present a case study of SENDAS by comparing the mobility patterns of millions of users during the COVID-19 pandemic period.

title: Is Circular Economy Always Sustainable? A System Dynamics Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Is Circular Economy Always Sustainable? A System Dynamics Approach
detail.abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) is often presented as a self-renewing system that minimizes waste, emissions, and energy loss through strategies of deceleration, closed material loops, and resource condensation. While CE promises resource efficiency and environmental benefits, its sustainability remains contested. Using Elkington’s Triple Bottom Line framework, this paper evaluates CE’s potential across resource efficiency, emission reduction, cost-effectiveness, and social equity. A review of existing literature highlights rapid academic interest but also reveals gaps: most studies emphasize environmental gains while neglecting social dimensions and long-term systemic resilience. This paper argues that CE cannot be assumed to be inherently sustainable; instead, its success depends on addressing conceptual ambiguities, practical limitations, and the integration of all three pillars of sustainability.

title: Holding the Bag: Depositor Reactions to a Crypto Shadow Bank Collapse

detail.title: Holding the Bag: Depositor Reactions to a Crypto Shadow Bank Collapse

detail.abstract: We study how customer characteristics shaped responses to the collapse of Celsius, a crypto platform that operated as a de facto bank. Linking bankruptcy filings to blockchain addresses, demographics, and cultural traits, we show that withdrawals reflected both monitoring capacity and informal mechanisms. Cultural heritage shaped behavior, with users from individualistic societies withdrawing earlier and more aggressively, while those from hierarchical societies delayed and left larger stranded balances. After withdrawals were frozen, users with greater stranded assets reduced activity but shifted their portfolios toward riskier tokens, consistent with gambling-for-resurrection behavior. Our findings show how both formal and informal monitoring mechanisms influence depositor behavior in shadow banking systems.

title: Development of a Comprehensive Management Framework for Design for Safety
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore (NUS) and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Development of a Comprehensive Management Framework for Design for Safety

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study as it did not involve clinical participants. All interviewees and focus group participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

detail.abstract: Design for Safety (DfS) offers a proactive strategy to address hazards during design to reduce accidents and ill health during construction, operations, maintenance, and demolition activities. However, current DfS regulations only provide broad duties and requirements, while DfS reviews operate as an isolated process that lacks a systemic approach. Hence, a critical gap exists in adopting a systems approach to DfS, where interconnected elements work cohesively to clearly define DfS goals and iteratively plan, execute, review, and improve the system to achieve better safety outcomes. Existing workplace safety and health management systems do not adequately address DfS requirements in sufficient detail, highlighting the need for a specialized framework. This research develops a comprehensive DfS management framework (DfSMF) through mixed-methods analysis of 61 peer-reviewed articles. The study identifies 25 critical success factors organized into nine elements mapped to ISO 45001. The three most significant elements, E3 Capability Support (contributing 19.58% to the total importance of the framework), E2 DfS Planning (17.57%), and E1 Leadership, Commitment, and Engagement (16.45%), collectively constitute over half of the total weighted importance score, demonstrating that human factors and systematic planning form the foundation of effective DfS implementation. The remaining elements include E8 Performance Evaluation, E6 System Support, E7 Design Risk Management, E9 Improvement, E5 DfS Tools Support, and E4 Resources, which serve as enablers rather than primary drivers of effective DfS. This evidence-based framework offers practical guidelines for effective management and continual improvement of DfS. The DfSMF transforms the current fragmented DfS approach into a holistic management system that enhances DfS outcomes and project performance.

title: A Set-Sequence Model for Time Series
affiliations: Stanford University, Amazon and Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering

detail.title: A Set-Sequence Model for Time Series
detail.abstract: Many prediction problems across science and engineering, especially in finance and economics, involve large cross-sections of individual time series, where each unit (e.g., a loan, stock, or customer) is driven by unit-level features and latent cross-sectional dynamics. While sequence models have advanced per-unit temporal prediction, capturing cross-sectional effects often still relies on hand-crafted summary features. We propose Set-Sequence, a model that learns cross-sectional structure directly, enhancing expressivity and eliminating manual feature engineering. At each time step, a permutation-invariant Set module summarizes the unit set; a Sequence module then models each unit's dynamics conditioned on both its features and the learned summary. The architecture accommodates unaligned series, supports varying numbers of units at inference, integrates with standard sequence backbones (e.g., Transformers), and scales linearly in cross-sectional size. Across a synthetic contagion task and two large-scale real-world applications-equity portfolio optimization and loan risk prediction-Set-Sequence significantly outperforms strong baselines, delivering higher Sharpe ratios, improved AUCs, and interpretable cross-sectional summaries.

detail.abstract: Cross-border OTC derivatives underpin global financial markets’ stability, thanks largely to the ISDA Master Agreement (MA), a paradigm of successful lex mercatoria. However, a string of lawsuits challenging cross-border derivatives’ validity shows that there are unsettled tensions. This article deep dives into those disputes, drawing three main lessons. First, the ISDA Master Agreement relies primarily on common law concepts, and on English (and New York) law and courts for support. This glosses over important differences with other jurisdictions on matters of risk ‘disclosure’, ‘advice’, or ‘capacity’, which are often enshrined in mandatory rules and legal principles and can shape contract enforceability. Second, the ISDA MA understandably protects itself from challenges to its enforceability through representations and warranties stating that the parties had ‘capacity’, that no ‘advice’ was provided, and that the parties understood and assumed all risks. Doing so, however, precludes a meaningful dialogue over differences of principle. Throughout the individual disputes courts have not managed to have a dialogue over these differences or find a compromise about the expectations regarding banks’ duties of disclosure of risks, or advice. Third, instead, ‘dialogue’ between legal systems has unfortunately focused on a discussion of non-bank counterparties’ “capacity” to conclude “speculative” transactions under their local laws. This was a bad choice. “Capacity” makes compromise impossible (an entity has it or lacks it, no matter of how careless it was) and determining whether an individual transaction is speculative is an uncertain, often futile exercise. Despite the unsatisfactory state, this litigation offers an opportunity to reflect about possible ways forward for derivatives’ lex mercatoria and governance.

detail.title: Economic Implications of the 2025 U.S.-India Tariff Dispute: A Comprehensive Analysis
detail.abstract: The 2025 U.S.-India tariff dispute is more than a short-term trade disagreement; it marks a turning point in one of the most significant economic relationships in the world. It all started with Washington's decision to impose steep tariffs on Indian imports in response to India's discounted purchases of Russian oil, disrupting trade flows, strained supply chains, and challenged household economies. India, where the U.S. accounts for nearly a fifth of exports, faces declining competitiveness, job losses in key industries such as textiles, jewelry, chemicals, and auto components, and a projected GDP slowdown of 0.3-0.5% (Times of India, 2025; Reuters, 2025). For American consumers, higher import costs essentially translate into an estimated additional $2,000-$2,400 per household per year (Dallas Federal Reserve, 2025). This study aims to bring together trade data, policy reports, and economic forecasts to analyze and assess the scale of the impact. The paper reviews existing literature on tariff policies and trade shocks, uses descriptive analysis of export and investment data, and discusses policy options for both countries. Findings suggest that while tariffs threaten India's export model, they may also accelerate diversification strategies and manufacturing reforms. On the U.S. side, consumer costs and strained diplomatic ties challenge the long-term sustainability of tariff-based policy. The policy implications include the need for effective diplomacy, and structural reforms to prevent temporary trade disputes from leaving permanent scars on the U.S. India partnership.

title: Balancing Compliance, Creativity, and Engagement: Evaluating the Impact of NSFW Governance on User Behaviors for Gen AI Platforms
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU), Pennsylvania State University - Department of Supply Chain & Information Systems, Wuhan University, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business and School of Computing and Artificial lntelligence

detail.title: Balancing Compliance, Creativity, and Engagement: Evaluating the Impact of NSFW Governance on User Behaviors for Gen AI Platforms
detail.abstract: Generative AI (Gen AI) platforms enable unprecedented creative output but also introduce new governance challenges, particularly in moderating Not Safe for Work (NSFW) content. This study examines how stricter NSFW governance affects user behavior and platform dynamics, using a natural experiment on a large text-to-image platform that implemented an external NSFW filter. Drawing on technology affordance theory (TAT), we conceptualize the stricter NSFW governance as a contraction of users' perceived action possibilities and investigate how users respond across three dimensions: subscription behavior, compliance adaptation, and content diversity. Our results show that stricter NSFW governance led to a 14% relative decline in subscription rates among users in the treatment group, reflecting economic disengagement due to a loss of affordance. Among those who remained, users reduced NSFW content and aligned with content policies, though content diversity was not significantly impaired. Furthermore, we find that NSFW attempts surged immediately after content blocking but declined over time, suggesting a phased process of affordance actualization. Finally, compliance varied across contexts, with mobile users showing weaker adaptation than PC users, and linked accounts exhibiting stronger behavioral adjustment. Theoretically, this work extends TAT to co-creative systems and demonstrates the temporal unfolding of governance-driven boundary internalization. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for designing governance strategies that balance platform safety, user creativity, and business sustainability.

detail.title: Fund Mergers, Cross-Ownership and Environmental Spillovers along Supply Chains
detail.abstract: This paper examines how vertical cross-ownership of customer-supplier pairs by socially responsible investors (SRIs) can promote suppliers' green transitions and stimulate attention to supply chain issues in other portfolio firms. We exploit mergers in which high-E-score mutual funds (E-funds) acquire non-E-fund targets, creating exogenous cross-ownership when customer firms are in the acquiring E-fund and their suppliers are in the target fund. Using a stacked difference-in-differences approach, we find that cross-owned suppliers improve their environmental performance significantly following such mergers. These improvements are driven by shifts in managerial attention and resources: the likelihood that acquiring funds mention supply chain issues in prospectuses and appoint managers or trustees with relevant expertise rises by 9.7% and 10.4%, respectively. Moreover, the cross-ownership acts as a catalyst that increases E-funds' awareness of supply chain risks across their portfolios, generating spillover effects on other suppliers, including those of newly acquired and pre-existing customer firms. Overall, our findings highlight ways in which cross-ownership enables SRIs to influence supply chain sustainability and generate meaningful spillover effects that range beyond directly held firms.

English Abstract

This paper proposes an operative model for the establishment of "The Civic Congress." While the first paper presented the theoretical and constitutional need for such a body, this paper focuses on the question of implementation: how to bridge the gap between theory and practice and build a civic association that will form the basis of the Congress. The starting point is the diagnosis that the current crisis stems not only from structural failures but from a systematic erosion of unwritten democratic norms. This process, identified with Francis Fukuyama's concept of "political decay," erodes trust and social capital in the country.


In response, the paper argues that the restoration of the political system lies in rebuilding social capital. The analysis is based on the insights of Mark E. Warren, who posits that democratic institutions must compensate for historical "failures of association." The paper demonstrates how the Israeli failure stems from a clash between "Bonding social capital" and "Bridging social capital," as defined by Robert Putnam. Therefore, this paper will expand on the social structure in Israel and the issue of representation for marginalized communities, delving into the origins of the societal rupture and its political manifestations, in order to compensate with economic-political influence against groups with "high cooperation."


Its function, based on sortition (random selection), will be to represent the individual and the voice of the people, free from political interests. The Congress could serve as a specific solution for acute crises in the system of governance, enable oversight and checks on all authorities, and even mandate institutional changes as needed. In doing so, it would grant the nation the institutional flexibility required to adapt its governing institutions to current norms. Beyond its representative role, the Civic Congress should be examined as a living mechanism and even as an independent "fourth branch of government" under the leadership of the President's Office, alongside the existing branches, to fully reflect the entirety of society and assist in resolving its crises.


The paper suggests two possible courses of action: The first is to build a dedicated body from the ground up, tasked with protecting and representing the interests of workers and various communities, thus forming the organizational basis for the Civic Congress. The second is to utilize existing organizations, presenting relevant and sustainable case studies that could grant the mechanism the required sovereignty.

detail.abstract: In the modern day’s fast-moving digital world, cloud computing has changed how we store, process, and retrieve data, letting companies and public agencies work together across continents almost without skipping a beat. Yet because the law usually moves slower than technology, officials now face a tangle of jurisdictional headaches-especially where the idea of data sovereignty comes into play. Since files can zip through many national borders and sit on far-flung servers, deciding which countries' rules apply and who really controls that information quickly turns into a heated legal debate. This paper sets out to unpack those jurisdictional puzzles, zeroing in on data sovereignty-the idea that digital material belongs to the legal order of the place where it physically rests. By comparing major treaties and home-grown laws, from Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation and America's CLOUD Act to China's Data Security Law, I show how competing views of national control and personal privacy are carving different regulatory paths. The worldwide reach of modern data laws-such as the GDPR-pulls cloud providers and their clients into a tangle of overlapping rules whenever they work across borders. The study therefore looks at supranational pacts and regional schemes, including the Councils 108+ Convention and fresh UN proposals, that try to fill these empty spaces. It points out, however, that such collective efforts often bump into solo moves by powerful states, leaving global firms with patchy rules they cannot easily follow. The paper pays special heed to the U.S. CLOUD Act, which lets American officials seize data kept abroad by U.S. companies and has sparked diplomatic spats and courtroom clashes over access. To ease matters, it weighs new tools-such as data-residency orders, updated mutual legal-assistance treaties, and broad digital-trade deals like CPTPP and DEPA-that might tame confusing jurisdictional lines. Yet national storage rules still aim to hold digital assets at home, and in doing so they can drain the speed, cost savings, and openness that make cloud commerce work, while also hinting at forms of digital protectionism. Lastly, this research advocates for a unified, objectives-oriented international legal framework which integrates national sovereignty into the international operational mechanisms. This would help in facilitating secure, interoperable, and privacy-conscious data flows when navigating cross-border cloud-computing complexities. This paper suggests the formation of a multilateral regulatory architecture based on the norms of transparency, accountability, and technological neutrality for reconciling sovereign interests with the inherently borderless nature of cloud technologies.

detail.abstract:
As enterprises accelerate their migration to SAP®S/4HANA, artificial intelligence is becoming a core feature of enterprise resource planning. Embedded AI scenarios such as predictive forecasting, automated cash application, and generative copilots (SAP® Joule) create new opportunities but also expose companies to unprecedented regulatory risks. The European Union’s AI Act (2025–2027), ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the GDPR, the Data Act, and sectoral rules such as DORA impose compliance duties not only on AI providers but increasingly on enterprise deployers. This paper introduces the SAP® AI Governance Compliance Framework, a governance model tailored to the SAP® ecosystem. It is designed to help organizations establish an audit-ready governance layer without modifying SAP® core systems. The framework consists of four pillars:

1. AI Use-Case Registry & Risk Classification – cataloging all SAP® AI scenarios and assessing risk levels. 2. RACI-Based Governance Roles – clarifying accountability across IT, compliance, and business functions. 3. Compliance Gap Analysis – mapping deployments to EU AI Act provisions, ISO/IEC 42001 controls, and data protection requirements. 4. Audit-Ready Documentation – standardized reporting for executives, auditors, and regulators. Unlike generic AI governance approaches, this framework is ERP-specific and provides a structured pathway toward AI Trust Labels and certification readiness. It bridges the gap between SAP®’s technological innovation and global compliance regimes, positioning itself as a potential industry standard for responsible AI in enterprise systems. By codifying governance into a measurable, replicable model, the SAP® AI Governance Compliance Framework enables organizations to scale AI responsibly, safeguard trust, and prepare for the regulatory milestones of 2025–2027. This framework should also be understood as a global contribution to AI governance, positioned as prior art and a reference model for enterprise-level AI compliance. Its logic is interoperable with OECD AI Principles, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and the G7 Hiroshima Process, underscoring its global relevance beyond the European regulatory space. This framework also serves as prior art for future standardization under ISO/IEC 42001 annexes and CEN/CENELEC harmonized standards. As enterprises accelerate their migration to SAP® S/4HANA, artificial intelligence is becoming a core feature of enterprise resource planning. Embedded AI scenarios such as predictive forecasting, automated cash application, and generative copilots (SAP® Joule) create new opportunities but also expose companies to unprecedented regulatory risks. The European Union’s AI Act (2025–2027), ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the GDPR, the Data Act, and sectoral rules such as DORA impose compliance duties not only on AI providers but increasingly on enterprise deployers. This paper introduces the SAP® AI Governance Compliance Framework, a governance model tailored to the SAP® ecosystem. It is designed to help organizations establish an audit-ready governance layer without modifying SAP® core systems. The framework consists of four pillars: (1) AI Use-Case Registry & Risk Classification, (2) RACI-Based Governance Roles, (3) Compliance Gap Analysis, and (4) Audit-Ready Documentation. Unlike generic AI governance approaches, this framework is ERP-specific and bridges the gap between SAP®’s technological innovation and global compliance regimes. By codifying governance into a measurable, replicable model, the SAP® AI Governance Compliance Framework enables organizations to scale AI responsibly, safeguard trust, and prepare for the regulatory milestones of 2025–2027. This framework establishes not only compliance readiness but provides prior art for de-facto standardization of ERP-based AI governance. We formalize an ERP-specific governance architecture for SAP® S/4HANA that aligns deployer obligations under the EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001 and OECD/NIST reference frameworks, and provide a replicable evidence model for audits and supervisory bodies. This framework operationalizes an audit-ready, zero-touch governance layer for SAP S/4HANA that maps deployer duties under the EU AI Act to ISO/IEC 42001 controls. Beyond compliance readiness, it establishes prior art for de-facto standardization of ERP-based AI governance.

title: Quiet Quitting as a Symptom: Testing the Role of HRM System Gaps Versus Motivational Decline

detail.title: Quiet Quitting as a Symptom: Testing the Role of HRM System Gaps Versus Motivational Decline
detail.abstract: Quiet quittingwhere employees meet basic job requirements but withdraw discretionary effortis an increasingly observed workplace phenomenon. This study examined whether quiet quitting is primarily a symptom of declining employee motivation or of gaps in the human resource management (HRM) system. A cross-sectional survey of 600 employees across multiple sectors in Lebanon was analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM). The integrated dual-path model achieved a good fit to the data (χ²/df = 2.48, CFI = 0.943, RMSEA = 0.059), indicating that the SEM results are within acceptable thresholds for model fit, and SEM results revealed partial support for H1(HRM system factors had a weaker direct effect), full support for H2 (intrinsic motivation was the strongest negative predictor of quiet quitting), and support for H3(Burnout significantly mediated the HRM gaps-quiet quitting link). Overall, quiet quitting was better explained by waning employee motivation than by HRM system deficiencies, though a lack of organizational support (e.g., low employee voice) still contributed. These findings underscore that quiet quitting represents both an individual coping response and a reaction to organizational shortcomings, highlighting the need for organizations to bolster employee engagement and well-being while addressing key HRM gaps to mitigate quiet quitting.
